And when a space starts thriving on parasocial loyalty, that problem gets worse. People stop responding to principle and start responding to proximity. They defend who they feel connected to. They excuse what they would condemn in others. They confuse audience attachment with moral clarity. That means none of us are exempt. Not believers, not atheists, not secular creators, not audience, not communities built around reason. The absence of religion does not save us from human hypocrisy. We are still capable of building our own little tribes, our own little priesthoods, our own little systems of loyalty, and selective outrage. We are still capable of using reason as branding while behaving in deeply irrational, self-serving, and unempathetic ways. So the challenge is bigger than leaving religion. The challenge is becoming the kind of people who can live ethically without hiding behind identity. Not I'm Christian, therefore I'm moral. Not I'm atheist, therefore I'm rational. Not I'm secular, therefore I care about people. None of those labels are enough. The real question is whether we are actually committed to reducing harm, telling the truth, resisting tribal distortion, and extending our moral concern beyond the people we like. Because empathy is not proven by what group you reject. It's proven by how you treat people when loyalty, ego, clout, and resentment are all pulling you in the other direction.
